newsitem.title: THAILAND: Ranariddh aide slams Hun Sen call for new co-premier.
newsitem.headline: Ranariddh aide slams Hun Sen call for new co-premier.

text.p: A senior aide to Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Monday rejected rival Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's call to name a new co-premier after two days of fighting in the capital Phnom Penh.
"Hun Sen has no right to issue such an illegal order," said Ranariddh's special envoy, Long Sarin, by telephone from the Thai-Cambodian border.
"Hun Sen came to power by force but FUNCINPEC came to power by the ballot."

FUNCINPEC is Ranariddh's royalist party which won the U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993 but which formed an uneasy coalition with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) after Hun Sen objected to the poll results.
The aide was referring to a statement by Hun Sen late on Sunday saying it was time for Cambodia to choose a new first prime minister.
The statement made late on Sunday followed clashes between forces loyal to the two premiers in the capital which killed at least 12 people and forced thousands to flee Phnom Penh.

"They (Hun Sen forces) control only Phnom Penh but forces loyal to the legal prime minister are still controlling most of the areas in the provinces. So it is not yet finished. This matter will be prolonged," Long Sarin said.
Hun Sen, whose CPP was the former communist government, said in a radio broadcast that the government was ready to choose a new First Prime Minister.
He said he did not want the job and that the new premier could be from FUNCINPEC.
Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn said on Monday Bangkok still recognised the coalition.

"At this moment we still recognise the coalition government," he said in a live television interview. "I hope that the Cambodian leaders will continue to abide by their constitution and any change involved will be confined to people" rather than the overall government.
A Thai army source said that forces loyal to Ranariddh were discussing forming a resistance force to fight Hun Sen with the support of Khmer Rouge guerrillas led by Khieu Samphan.
Ranariddh had been negotiating with Khieu Samphan on a possible political role for the guerrillas. Hun Sen had called the negotiations illegal.
The source, based in Aranyaprathet, bordering the Cambodian town of Poipet, said Ranariddh's forces had disarmed Hun Sen loyalists at the border town and taken control.
"There are about 300 fresh reinforcements of FUNCINPEC troops deployed to control the border town now," the source said.
The Australian defence attache to Cambodia, Colonel David Mead, told Reuters on Sunday the situation in northwestern Cambodia was tense between the rival forces.
